utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask the Registrar to call the case, please? THE CLERK OF THE COURT: Case number 95-14-AR-108 bis, Prosecutor versus Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ARBOUR
utterances.text: Good morning, I am Louise Arbour, I am the Prosecutor, and with me is Mr Mark Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MULJACIC
utterances.text: Good morning, I am the Croatian Ambassador here in the Kingdom of the Netherlands. To my left is, Orsat Miljenic, First Secretary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have been informed by counsel for General Blaskic that they have waived their right to attend the delivery of the judgement of the Appeals Chamber and that he appears unrepresented on this occasion. May I ask General Blaskic whether he can hear me? THE DEFENDANT: Good morning, Messrs Presidents, I can hear you well and I can understand you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. You can be seated. THE DEFENDANT: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I should like to say that Judge Li and Judge Vohrah I am afraid are unable to attend this hearing and have asked me to extend their apologies. You may remember that at the close of the hearing of the 22nd September I promised to deliver this judgement within three weeks. Unfortunately this has proved impossible. It was too great a task, as the issues with which we have grappled are difficult and complex. I therefore apologise for not keeping my word. There is, however, another reason for our failure to deliver on time, one reason which some may feel excuses this delay. My colleagues and I are pleased to be able to render this judgement of the Appeals Chamber both in English and French, the two official languages of the International Tribunal. This significant achievement I should note has been made possible by the dedication and competence of our translators who have provided an excellent French translation. May I add that this is the first time that the judgement, a judgement of the International Criminal Tribunal is delivered simultaneously in both languages. I will now read slowly a short summary of our judgement. As you know, this matter has come before the Appeals Chamber by way of an appeal by the Republic of Croatia against the decision of Trial Chamber II on 18th July, 1997, upholding the issuance to Croatia and its Minister of Defence of a subpoena duces tecum and this subpoena duces tecum was issued by Judge McDonald on 15th January, 1997, in connection with the case of Prosecutor versus Blaskic which is currently being heard by Trial Chamber I. In oral submissions to the Appeals Chamber on the 22nd September, and in its written pleadings, the Republic of Croatia has questioned the power of our International Tribunal to issue orders designated as subpoena duces tecum to Croatia, or to any other sovereign State, and also to high state officials. After careful deliberation the Appeals Chamber has unanimously reached a decision on this matter, and has issued a judgement which I shall now briefly summarise. The Appeals Chamber has first of all dealt with two preliminary issues, namely the legal meaning of the term "subpoena", and whether the question of legal remedies in case of non-compliance with orders or subpoenas was ripe for consideration by the Appeals Chamber. As for the first issue, namely the legal meaning of the term "subpoena", the Appeals Chamber holds that this term should be construed as referring only and exclusively to binding orders addressed by the International Tribunal under threat of penalty to individuals, acting in their private capacity. With respect to the other issue, namely whether the question of legal remedies is ripe for consideration, the Appeals Chamber has found that it is inappropriate to resort to the doctrine of ripeness in these proceedings. Whatever the merits of this domestic law doctrine, a doctrine upheld, as you know, in the USA, it appears to the Appeals Chamber to be inapposite to transpose it into international criminal proceedings. Furthermore, it is wrong to suggest that the issue of legal remedy is not ripe for judicial consideration given the extent to which it has been debated by the parties before the Appeals Chamber. After consideration of these preliminary issues, the Appeals Chamber has reached an unanimous decision on all of the four matters which it has identified as the core issues in this dispute. The first question is whether the International Tribunal is empowered to issue subpoena and binding orders to States, to sovereign States. Here the Appeals Chamber holds that subpoenae, in the sense of injunctions accompanied by threat of penalty, cannot, cannot be issued to States. The International Tribunal does not possess any power to take enforcement measures against sovereign States. Such powers cannot be regarded as inherent to the functions of an international judicial body such as our Tribunal. Under current international law, States can only be the subject of countermeasures taken by other States or of sanctions visited upon them by the international organised community, that is to say the United Nations or other intergovernmental organisations. Had the drafters of our Statute intended to vest the International Tribunal with such a power contrary to current international law, they would have expressly provided for it. By contrast, binding orders or requests can be addressed to States. Article 29 of our Statute requires all States to cooperate and lend judicial assistance to the International Tribunal. This obligation is reiterated in paragraph 4 of Security Council resolution 827(1993). Its binding force thus derives from the provisions of Chapter VII and Article 25 of the United Nations Charter, and from the Security Council resolution adopted pursuant to those provisions of the UN Charter. This exceptional legal basis accounts for the novel and indeed unique power granted to the International Tribunal to issue orders to sovereign States. Article 29 of our Statute sets out a clear obligation which is incumbent on every Member State of the United Nations, every member State of United Nations. Article 29 also posits a community interest in its observance. As for the question of legal remedies available in case of non-compliance by a State with a binding order or request, the Appeals Chamber holds that it is for the International Tribunal's parent body, the Security Council, to impose sanctions, if any, against a recalcitrant State, under the conditions provided for in Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter. However, our Tribunal is endowed with the inherent power to make a judicial finding concerning a State's failure to observe the provisions of the Statute or the Rules. It also has the power to report this judicial finding to the Security Council. Where such a report is made, the Security Council will decide whether or not to take any action against the recalcitrant State. In addition, subject to certain conditions, each Member State of the United Nations may act upon the communal legal interest in the observance of this international obligation laid down in Article 29. A collective response through other intergovernmental organisations may also be envisaged, again subject to certain strict conditions. The second question the Appeals Chamber has considered is the question of whether the International Tribunal is empowered to issue subpoenae and/or binding orders to States or officials. The Appeals Chamber holds that the International Tribunal may not address subpoena to state officials acting in their official capacity. Such officials are mere instruments of a State, and their official action can only be attributed to the State. It is a well-established rule of customary international law that they cannot be the subject of sanctions or penalties for conduct that is not private but undertaken on behalf of that State. The Appeals Chamber also finds that both under general international law and our Statute itself Judges or Trial Chambers cannot address binding orders to States or officials. It follows that if a Judge or a Chamber intends to order the production of documents, the seizure of evidence, the arrest of suspects, et cetera, being acts involving action by a State, its organs or officials, the Judge or the Chamber must turn to the relevant State for assistance. The third question tackled by the Appeals Chamber is that of whether the International Tribunal may issue binding orders to individuals acting in their private capacity. The Appeals Chamber finds that the International Tribunal can issue binding orders in the form of subpoenae, that is under threat of penalty to individuals acting in their private capacity. This power derives from the general object and purpose of the Statute, as well as the role that the International Tribunal is called upon to play thereunder. These factors, as well as the relevant provisions, confer on the International Tribunal an incidental or ancillary jurisdiction over individuals other than those whom the Tribunal may prosecute and try under its primary jurisdiction. These are individuals who may be of assistance in the task of dispensing criminal justice entrusted to our Tribunal. As for the legal remedies for non-compliance by individuals, the Appeals Chamber is of the opinion that the Tribunal should normally turn to the relevant national authorities to seek remedies or sanctions for non-compliance by an individual with an order or subpoenae issued by a Judge or a Trial Chamber. Legal remedies or sanctions put in place by the national authorities themselves are indeed more likely to work effectively and expeditiously. However, allowance should be made for cases where resort to national remedies or sanctions is not feasible. In such cases the remedies available to the International Tribunal should be utilised. These remedies range from a general power to hold individuals in contempt of the International Tribunal, utilising the inherent contempt power rightly mentioned by the Trial Chamber to the specific contempt power provided for in Rule 77 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The fourth and last question considered by the Appeals Chamber is that of national security concerns. The Appeals Chamber recognises that customary international rules do protect the national security of States by prohibiting every State from interfering with, or intruding into, the domestic jurisdiction, including national security matters of other States. However, the Statute imposes upon all States the obligation among other things to provide to the International Tribunal documents germane to the conduct of trials. This is an extremely and innovative sweeping obligation which clearly derogates from general international law. Had the founding fathers intended to place restrictions upon these powers of the International Tribunal, they would have done so expressly. This Chamber has been persuaded by the submissions of the Prosecutor that to grant States a blanket right to withhold documents necessary for a trial might jeopardise the very function of the International Tribunal, and, as she put it, defeat its essential object and purpose. Recognition of such a right to use national security concerns to withhold documents could lead to the stultification of international criminal proceedings as they might prove crucial to the determination of innocence or guilt. The very raison d’être of the International Tribunal would be undermined. Nevertheless, the Appeals Chamber emphasises that the International Tribunal should be alert to legitimate national security concerns of States. The Trial Chamber rightly indicated that the best way of reconciling the conflicting interests of the International Tribunal and the State would be to hold in camera ex parte proceedings in order to scrutinise the validity of its national security claims, of States' national security claims. The Appeals Chamber, whilst in broad agreement with the Trial Chamber, suggests in addition several practical methods and procedures to guide this process of scrutiny. These methods and procedures include consideration of the degree of bona fide co-operation and assistance lent by the relevant States to our Tribunal, as well as the general attitude of the State vis-à-vis the International Tribunal, whether it is opposed to the fulfilment of its functions or instead consistently supports and assists our Tribunal. The majority of the Appeals Chamber also suggests that the relevant documents could be submitted through the scrutiny of one Judge, one Judge of the Trial Chamber, designated by the Trial Chamber itself. Judge Karibi-Whyte has appended a separate opinion on this question of the scrutiny of the national security concerns by the International Tribunal. It is his view that such scrutiny should be undertaken by the whole Trial Chamber and not by a single Judge. Of course it will be for the relevant Trial Chamber to decide whether to adopt any of the methods or procedures suggested by our Appeals Chamber, or to provide for other practical arrangements or protective measures if need be, in consultation with the interested States. I shall now read the disposition of our judgement. It reads as follows: "The Appeals Chamber unanimously finds: "(1) That the International Tribunal is empowered to issue binding orders and requests to States which are obliged to comply with them pursuant to Article 29 of the Statute, and that in case of non-compliance a Trial Chamber may make a specific judicial finding to this effect and request the President of the International Tribunal to transmit it to the United Nations Security Council. "(2) The Appeals Chamber unanimously finds that the International Tribunal may not address binding orders under Article 29 to state officials acting in their official capacity. "(3) The Appeals Chamber unanimously finds that the International Tribunal may summon, subpoena or address other binding orders to individuals acting in their private capacity, and that in case of non-compliance either the enforcement measures provided for in the relevant State may be taken or the International Tribunal may instigate contempt proceedings. "(4) The Appeals Chamber unanimously finds that States are not allowed, are not allowed on the claim of national security interests to withhold documents and other evidential material requested by the International Tribunal. However, practical arrangements may be adopted by a Trial Chamber to make allowance for legitimate and bona fide concerns of States. "(5) The Appeals Chamber unanimously decides to quash the subpoena duces tecum issued by Judge McDonald and reinstated it by Trial Chamber II addressed to Croatia and the Croatian Defence Minister Mr Gojko Susak it being understood that the Prosecutor is at liberty to submit to the appropriate Chamber, being Trial Chamber I, a request for a binding order addressed to Croatia alone." That is all. The hearing is therefore adjourned.
